title: The Missing Treaty and the War over Entrance Music
subtitle: Mystery, investigation and classic adventures

opening.title: The Veterans Have Seen My Welcome Package
paragraphs: “Nigga, why have you declared war at a hotel?” Shawna asked.

The banner was still rolled up. That should have bought me time. Unfortunately, my wife could read the invoice. THE SECOND GREAT BUTCH VS. STUD WAR occupied its own line, directly above PREMIUM UNFURLING ASSISTANCE. I explained that war was a metaphor. She pointed at the next line. “Then why does your metaphor need a smoke machine?”

Auntie June arrived before I could develop a defense. Eighty-two, retired bus driver, Black butch lesbian, blue suit sharp enough to separate me from my excuses. Odessa, whom everyone called Dez, followed with a garment bag over one arm. Eighty-four, retired seamstress, Black stud lesbian, looking at June like she'd been returning the same overdue library book for fifty-nine years.

“The first war wasn't about the jukebox,” June said immediately. “It was about principle.” Dez took off her glasses. “It was about you putting your song on six times.” “People liked it.” “People left, nigga.” The legendary Blue Comet Social Club feud of 1967 had three surviving accounts, all contradicted by the two surviving people telling them. There was a borrowed jacket, a hall-rental agreement each swore the other had never signed, and a peace dinner that apparently ran out of potato salad before peace could develop.

I had heard this story at a cookout and made the reasonable leap to hiring a casino convention floor. My invitation promised rival entrances, a game night, and a coalition summit to settle unfinished business. June had accepted because she wanted to hear her song on a good system. Dez had accepted with June's jacket in her garment bag and a counterclaim about decades of excellent alterations. Everybody else had accepted because I'd said there would be food and interesting games. The relationship between those objectives and my budget was already deteriorating.

Rae arrived with a bike helmet under her arm and examined the signing table before saying hello. Black stud, mechanic, detective-story enthusiast, a woman capable of diagnosing a wobble from six feet away. Kit came behind her carrying a karaoke folder and asking where her blue entrance light was. White butch, librarian, soft voice, powerful opinions about a chorus. I gave them separate welcome packets. Kit opened hers. “Mine says we're bitter rivals.” Rae looked at the crackers. “I'm bitter about these.” They went together to find better ones.

Nia, a Black trans lesbian and femme, had received two packets, one for the lesbian caucus and one for the trans delegation. “Do I get two dinners?” she asked. “Only if you can carry both,” Rosa said. Nia smiled and stayed near Rae, who was making an excellent argument for actual olives. The contract lawyer had promised to inspect our evening's agreement. She had not promised to spend her whole night lawyering. Her other objective was a dance, though she hadn't yet decided how to ask for it.

Mika, our trans nonbinary event planner, put a tiny model hotel beside the registration tablet. “For scale,” they said. I thought they meant my ambition. They meant the floor plan. Velvet Payroll, a Black drag queen with exquisite timing, swept in with a garment rack and a payment schedule. Remy, a trans man whose drag-king name was King Receipts, followed with a crown and the world's most aggressively cheerful fanfare. Velvet needed stage time. Remy needed a microphone that worked. Mercedes needed both of them to let her finish soundcheck. Porsche needed me away from the recording equipment.

Shawna took my hand. “I need my husband for part of tonight.” I assured her that the husband was in exceptional operating condition. “Then stop leasing him to your own decorations.” She looked beautiful, amused, and very close to putting me in a cupboard until I could behave.

Mika handed Rosa the silver folder while she cleared registration. Somewhere in that transfer I decided the welcome sign needed a stiffer backing. Elsewhere, I put the ceremonial pen down while checking my portrait. These were small decisions. History enjoys waiting until small decisions have become expensive before telling you which ones mattered.

June and Dez took chairs beside the first mystery game. The banner came down crooked. Tank stared at it, then at me. “These niggas wanted a party. You bought them a sequel.” I reached for the folder to explain the agenda. It was gone. The pen was gone too. Shawna smiled without mercy. “There. First mystery.”

games.case_title: The Ghost Delegation Has Arrived
scene: I reserved a seat for Joey Mallone because Blackwell had a ghost partner and our summit had an attendance minimum. One more delegate could keep the hotel from charging for empty chairs.
Rae lifted his name card. “Does he want chips?” “He transcends appetite.” Tank reached around her. “Then he transcends these.”

Kit was trying to hang her entrance banner without covering the screen. Her reading glasses slid down her nose. She pushed them up, looked at Joey's chair, and asked whether an invisible guest also needed an entrance song.
“Something haunting,” I said. Mercedes played three notes from the invoice notification on my phone. The whole fucking room recognized it.
Our Rosa watched the medium get another unwanted responsibility. “That's my supernatural power too.” She handed me the catering form. I tried passing it to the ghost delegation.
Rae sat in Joey's empty chair and held the screen steady for Kit. Tank kept the chips. Nigga, even the dead were organizing more effectively than me.
games.pleasure: A compact New York supernatural mystery joins a reluctant medium to a sardonic spirit guide. Conversations and notebook connections make discovery feel personal; the developing partnership offers more reason to continue than simply clearing another puzzle.
games.burden: Notebook combinations, returning to locations, and remembering names remain real work. Suicide and bereavement are central. Reviews report no timed or dexterity challenges, but this is not a complete-path playtest. Current desktop patches offer manual speech advance through a Ctrl+P toggle; verify it waits.

games.ruling: The ghost partnership may earn your curiosity; follow the plain notes first. At our summit, the invisible delegate has already lost both his vote and his snacks.

games.case_title: The Haunting Has a Lighting Rider
scene: Kit wanted blue light for her entrance. Rae wanted enough ordinary light to find the signing table. I promised both and pressed the button marked ATMOSPHERE.
The ballroom went purple. A motor groaned behind the curtain. Tank said, “Nigga, your atmosphere sounds like it owes money.”

We had The Darkside Detective on a monitor, which encouraged me to identify the groan as a paranormal case. Mika opened the curtain. My rented revolving platform was trying to turn beneath a refrigerator.
“That isn't a ghost,” they said. “That's your champagne presentation.” I said presentations required mystery. Rae unplugged it before the mystery required a fire report.
Kit found a separate lamp and aimed it at the table. Then she restored her blue entrance light. Two useful decisions, neither of which required me to say haunting again.
Remy tried the microphone. “Spirits are high.” Velvet closed her eyes. “Baby, save something for the people who aren't trapped here.” I paid the refrigerator's appearance fee.

games.case_title: Objection, the Host Has Bought Another Entrance
scene: Nia saw Phoenix Wright on the screen and asked why my hotel bill described a SECOND TRIUMPHAL ARRIVAL. I said the first triumph had gone well in rehearsal.
“You haven't arrived once,” Shawna said. “You've been here all afternoon.” “Emotionally, baby.” “Financially, too.”
Rae wanted the receipt entered into evidence. Kit objected because her entrance music had been charged to the same line. Suddenly the rival caucuses shared a fascinating concern about itemization.
I pointed at Nia. “You're a lawyer. Defend me.” She looked at the receipt. “I'm off duty, and the witness has written his confession in gold foil.”
Remy struck a small gong for order. Its handle came off in his hand. Velvet took the gong away and gave him a spoon. Nobody let me call a recess.
The verdict was simple: one entrance per actual arrival. Kit got her music separated from my nonsense. Rae saved a chair beside Nia. Nigga, the defense had plans after court.

games.case_title: The Plant Shop Has a Catering Complaint
scene: Strange Horticulture inspired me to label the centerpieces with mysterious Latin names. Rosa read one card and asked why I was serving sandwiches beside Something Possibly Fatal.
“Atmosphere.” “Move your fucking atmosphere away from my bread.”

Rae wanted fresh mint for the water. Kit wanted the fern removed from her sightline to the stage. I said the plants were participants in the occult experience. Shawna asked whether the fern had paid a deposit.
Nia inspected my labels. Every scientific name was a cocktail. She turned over the nearest card. “This plant is apparently a Double Manhattan.”
Mercedes took the labels for song requests. Mika moved the tall centerpiece onto a low side table, where it promptly looked better. I pretended that had been my second design proposal.

Rae brought Nia a glass with actual mint. Nia thanked her without making a speech. I tried offering Shawna a botanical surprise. “If that means another fern in our suite, nigga, surprise somebody else.”

games.burden: Books, plants, labels, letters, and a map can create substantial cross-referencing. Desk objects use dragging; a developer patch added a double-click sticky-drag alternative, whose own double-click demand needs testing. Wrong answers raise Rising Dread and can lead to a recovery puzzle. Calm presentation is not simplicity.

games.ruling: The plant shop's close observation may appeal, while dragging and cross-referencing deserve a trial. Our centerpiece survived only after its mysterious identity stopped threatening the sandwiches.

games.case_title: The Golden Idol Has My Chin
scene: I unveiled the centerpiece statue while The Case of the Golden Idol filled the monitor. A bronze-looking man stood on a little plinth, one hand raised toward destiny.
Tank leaned close. “Nigga, that's you.” “An idealized statesman.” “They idealized your stomach.”

Kit found a red velvet rope around it and assumed something valuable had been stolen. Rae said something valuable had definitely disappeared from the budget. Nia asked whether the figure could hold the missing treaty pen.
I placed a pen in its raised hand. The hand bent forward. My idealized statesman now appeared to be demanding a gratuity from a fern.
Velvet examined the plinth. “It rotates?” “For the reveal.” “Put my spotlight on it.” She stepped onto the nearby floor mark and transformed my unveiling into a rehearsal for her number.
Mika let her finish before telling me the statue blocked a cable route. We moved it. Nigga, the first conspiracy in the room was everybody discovering a better use for my monument.

games.case_title: The Automaton Is in the Coat Room
scene: Syberia's mechanical world made me regret nothing about hiring a clockwork-looking greeter. It stood beside registration with brass shoulders, a little hat, and one excellent prerecorded welcome.
Rae walked past it. “Welcome, distinguished chairman.” She stopped. “No.” I said the greeting was generic. “So is the refund request,” she said.
Mika opened its panel while Kit examined the gear decorations. Most of them were glued on. The entire mechanical wonder was a speaker wearing an expensive coat.
Shawna pressed the next button. “Welcome, distinguished chairman,” it said again, louder. Tank put a bread roll in its open hand. “Nigga needs something to do.”
We found the actual welcome recording on my phone. Mercedes had made it that morning. Warm, brief, no chairman. I had forgotten to send it because I was choosing epaulettes.
Mika replaced the audio. Rae carried the greeter to the coat room, where it welcomed everyone perfectly. My mechanical empire advanced through a cable and an apology.

games.case_title: Everybody Brought a Different Kind of Trouble
scene: Unavowed's companions had different histories and abilities. I announced that our coalition also required a specially selected team. Nia asked whether I meant the people already doing the work.
“Exactly. I recognized their potential.” “After they carried your statue.”

Rae could fix the signing table's wobble. Kit knew where the spare lamps were. Mika had the floor manager's actual number. I offered charisma. Tank offered to carry charisma outside if it kept talking.

Velvet wanted a team for her costume change, which sounded much more glamorous. I volunteered immediately. She handed me a garment steamer and pointed at the crease I had just made by leaning against her cape.
Shawna watched me concentrate. “Look at that. An ability.” I said I had several she knew intimately. “Keep one of them on the fabric, baby.”
By the time the crease vanished, Rae had fixed the table and Kit had found the missing pen cap. The team advanced. Its founder was still untangling a cord.

games.case_title: Her Testimony Has a Better Search Term
scene: Her Story made everyone interested in searching a statement by one revealing word. I suggested we search my welcome video for vision. Porsche searched for refundable.
Nothing came up. Tank whispered, “Nigga, that's the mystery.”

The missing treaty had last appeared in a clip I recorded beside the registration desk. We watched me lift a folder, praise my own foresight, then hand it off without looking. The recipient was outside the frame.
Kit asked for the next clip. I had recorded my shoes instead. Rae admired the sheer consistency of a man documenting everything except useful information.
Nia noticed a silver cuff at the edge of the image. Velvet held up both wrists. “These are gold, counselor. Don't implicate affordable jewelry in my affairs.”

Shawna found a later photograph. Mika had the folder, but the photograph didn't show where it went next. I proposed another speech to establish context. Six people said no with strikingly different levels of affection.

games.case_title: The Burial Mound Is a Coat Pile
scene: Hob's Barrow gave our investigation a moody turn. I found a suspicious mound behind the stage and told Rae we might be dealing with a deliberately concealed chamber.
She lifted a sleeve. “We're dealing with coats.” “People conceal things in coats.” “Usually their arms, nigga.”
Kit insisted one coat contained her missing glasses. They were on her head. She removed them, thanked Rae very quietly, and then accused me of burying her entrance banner beneath the mound.
The banner was there. So was a pair of shoes, three abandoned welcome bags, and Remy's little crown. He emerged from rehearsal demanding to know why the monarchy had been interred.
Velvet put the crown on him crooked. “Historical accuracy.” Remy bowed, knocked the banner loose, and revealed the hotel map we'd been trying to find.
I claimed the excavation as a success. Rosa handed me the coats. “Then carry your findings to the fucking coat room.” Archaeology had developed a surprisingly personal labor requirement.

games.case_title: The Illuminated Agenda Costs Extra
scene: Pentiment's historical art prompted me to order an illuminated agenda. Gold initials, curling vines, a drawing of the summit founder in a position of modest authority.
Kit unfolded it. “That's a throne.” “Modest for a throne.”

Rae wanted to know when the games started. The agenda began with a poem about my generosity. Nia traced a beautiful vine across the paper until it ended at a blank space where the start time should have been.
Mika wrote the time in pencil. I protested that the calligrapher had a vision. “So do the caterers,” they said. “It involves leaving before breakfast.”

Mercedes liked the border and asked whether she could use it around her set list. Velvet requested the tiny portrait for a joke during her number. Suddenly my commission had three practical uses, none involving the poem.
Shawna folded the agenda into her bag. “I'm keeping this.” I smiled. “Sentimental?” “Evidence. Nigga, the next romantic weekend is a beach and two towels.”

games.case_title: The Time Agent Wants Yesterday's Rate
scene: Old Skies put time travel within professional reach. I asked Nia whether a contract could be renegotiated yesterday. She said yesterday I should have read it.
“Nigga, that's what I'm proposing.” “You're proposing a time machine because you rented six chandeliers.”
Mika loved the chandeliers. This surprised everyone until they arranged three over the dance floor and admitted the room looked spectacular. Kit wanted the other three behind her karaoke entrance.
Rae pointed at the empty signing table. “Could one future include a lamp here?” Nia brought her a lamp. She also brought a chair and stayed in it, which seemed like a promising use of the present.
Shawna asked what I would change if we could travel backward. I said I would meet her sooner. She softened. Then I added that we could have booked the room before the weekend surcharge.
Her look traveled several years into my future. “Start over,” she said. I did, using fewer dates and absolutely no pricing information.

Temporal cause and effect can increase memory demands, and later timing, dragging, and dialogue advance need an edition-specific check. Some historical settings carry serious emotional weight.

games.case_title: The Robot Has Applied for Independence
scene: Primordia's robot partnership had me considering a future without the hotel manager. Mika pointed out that most hotel problems in our room originated with a human called Aiden.
I directed attention to my electronic welcome podium. Its screen read UPDATE REQUIRED. Tank said, “Nigga, even your furniture wants a new host.”
Rae opened the little cupboard beneath it and found six charging cables, all for something else. Remy tried speaking through its built-in microphone. The podium answered with a piercing squeal.
Velvet took his arm. “Come sing with the living, baby.” He went immediately, carrying his victory fanfare on a tiny keyboard. A machine had lost a romantic man to a better sound system.
Kit fetched a handwritten sign from registration. Clear lettering, correct room, actual times. She propped it against the dead screen and reclaimed her lamp.
I asked whether the podium could remain as a symbol. Rosa set a water pitcher on it. “Now it symbolizes water.” The post-human future had an unexpectedly sensible refreshment policy.

The inspected storefront does not certify zero timers, no holds, or a particular text-wait setting; those remain checks, not benefits to assume.

Shawna opened the folder. The first page said DRAFT AGENDA. No treaty yet. I had successfully lost a document that hadn't even reached the level of commitment I was claiming.

games.case_title: The Biker Declines My Cavalcade
scene: Full Throttle's road-movie attitude made me ask Rae to lead a ceremonial motorcade around the hotel entrance. She looked at me, then at the newly recovered agenda.
“Does the agenda say motorcade?” “It could.” “Then keep the fucking pen away from him,” she told Nia.

Remy wanted to arrive on something impressive. Velvet offered him the little wheeled costume trunk. He sat on it with his crown perfectly straight while Tank pushed him six feet and demanded a transport fee.
Kit played his victory fanfare. It was terrible, triumphant, and exactly as requested. Remy grinned so widely that nobody suggested replacing it with something tasteful.
Rae put her bike lock back in her bag. Nia asked whether she could show her the bike later. “If you like,” Rae said, suddenly less fluent than she'd been about every snack in the room.
I offered to organize their viewing. Shawna took my arm. “You got an appointment with me, nigga.” For once I followed the correct person through the correct door.

interludes.title: The First War Had a Jacket and the Second Had a Default Setting
paragraphs: June put a photograph on the table during the break. Four women stood outside the Blue Comet in 1967, grinning beside a car whose hood occupied most of the street. Dez touched the corner carefully. June pointed at her own shoulders.
“My jacket.”

“Our jacket,” Dez said. Rae made a low appreciative sound. Nia pulled up a chair. I reached for a microphone. Shawna took it out of my hand before anybody needed to explain why two elderly women discussing a photograph didn't require amplification.

June had bought the jacket with money she'd saved. Dez had borrowed it, altered it, and developed a theory of ownership based on how often people complimented her in it. At one point she'd returned something she described as equivalent. “It was brown,” Dez said. “So was the jacket.” June stared at her. “Aiden, this nigga returned a cardigan.” Tank nearly inhaled an olive. Kit sat down so quickly her glasses slid into her lap.

Dez insisted the cardigan had pockets. June said pockets weren't restitution. Remy wanted to know whether this dispute had inspired the original peace agreement. June said the agreement came after somebody interrupted her jukebox song. Dez said June remembered paying for the record and forgot who'd had the taste to select it. Both claimed the other had left the agreement unsigned.
Kit studied the photograph. “I thought the first rivalry was supposed to explain ours.”
June looked at her. “Which one is ours?”

Kit glanced between herself and Rae, then at the invitation. The design had helped her reach the wrong answer. White butch on one side, Black stud on the other, although my words had not stated it quite that plainly. I had put the faces in separate colored panels and trusted implication to perform the labor I couldn't defend aloud. June, a Black butch sitting directly between them, had become a very expensive problem for my layout.
“I know those aren't mutually exclusive categories,” Kit said. “I didn't invent his fucking invitation.”
“No,” Rae said. “But when he called you the butch representative, you took the good chair.”

Kit's jaw shifted. I recognized the look: a person finding one true detail inside an accusation and desperately wanting to negotiate the rest before acknowledging it. I had worn that look through three vehicle inspections. “I took the chair because I was carrying the music folder. You could have asked for it.”
“Why did I have to ask you?”
The room got quiet in a different way. Not reverent. Uncomfortable. My instinct was to buy something that made a noise. Shawna put her hand on my wrist without looking at me.

Kit said she hadn't felt particularly powerful arriving at an event where the host expected her to be a mascot. At the library she still heard people soften their voices before asking whether she worked in maintenance. She knew what it was to be stared at, to have a woman pull her child closer, to see her clothes become somebody else's public question. “So when you say I just get to be the default, I don't know where that person lives. I'd like her rent.”

Rae let her finish. “I'm not saying nobody does shit to you. I'm saying the hotel guy asked you where you wanted the lamp. He asked me which door the contractors were using. Same shoes, same table, same invitation in my hand.”
Kit looked toward the corridor. She'd been present for that exchange. “I thought he meant because you were fixing it.”

“He hadn't seen me fix anything.” Rae wasn't loud. That made it harder for me to hope the moment would dissolve into ordinary party noise. “You don't have to invent my experience out of yours before it counts.”

June tapped the photograph. “And don't make me disappear so the argument fits two columns. I've been a Black butch longer than either of y'all has been deciding what to call this seating arrangement.”
Dez smiled. “She was a difficult Black butch before breakfast too.” June nudged her knee. The laugh loosened the room without cancelling anything that had been said.

I tried explaining that I wanted the invitation to feel bold. Rae turned it over. “Bold for whom, nigga? You get a funny war. I get assigned a whole personality before I even complain about the crackers.”

That landed because she had complained about the crackers. I had treated the complaint as perfect character confirmation: of course my stud delegate arrived ready to inspect the room. The fact was less convenient. Rae was a mechanic, liked things that worked, and had been served terrible crackers. I had converted three ordinary facts into a costume that supposedly explained her.

“Stud is a word I learned from Black women who made room for me,” Rae said. “It means something to me. It isn't a menu where you order confidence, tools, and whatever voice you think goes with them.” She paused. “And yes, I brought tools. I'm not giving them back just to defeat your symbolism.”

Kit laughed once, then stopped trying to make Rae laugh on her behalf. “I liked being introduced without having to explain myself,” she said. “That's the part I don't want to admit. You said butch like the room would know what to do with me, and I liked it. I didn't ask who you were making explain the rest.”

Rae nodded. It wasn't absolution. Kit didn't demand any. She took off the little ribbon I'd pinned to her chair and laid it on the table. Then she asked whether Rae actually wanted that chair. “No. I want the one beside Nia.” Rae realized she'd said it plainly and reached for her water too quickly. Nia looked delighted and had the decency to examine her glass instead of conducting a public hearing.

Remy leaned back. “Can I put in one request? Don't turn masculinity into a staircase with me at the top because I'm a man.” He adjusted his tiny crown. “I spent forty minutes trying to glue this straight. Nobody should be aspiring upward into this particular crisis.”
Velvet straightened it with two fingers. “There, your majesty. Social progress.”

He smiled. “Somebody sees Rae, then Kit, then me, and wants one explanation for all of us. It saves them asking a person anything. I'm a trans man. My drag king is a performance. Those aren't interchangeable with being a butch woman, and being a man doesn't make me better at the microphone.”
“Nothing could,” Velvet said tenderly. He kissed her hand in theatrical gratitude for the review.

Kit looked at Rae's jacket. “For the record, that shoulder line is beautiful.” Rae smiled. “Your suit too. You look like you know exactly which song you want.” Kit sat a little taller. She liked her shape in those clothes; Rae liked hers. No correction was required. June watched them with satisfaction. “Looking good is allowed to be part of the politics, babies. Otherwise Dez owes me fifty-nine years of evidence for why she kept borrowing the damn jacket.”

Kit admitted she sometimes felt pushed to prove her masculinity by being unbothered. Don't ask for help. Don't enjoy the wrong song. Don't look too excited when somebody pretty notices you. “I've had gay male friends understand the performance part beautifully, and one tell me I was basically a junior version of him. I told him he couldn't afford my subscription.”

Rae said her friendships with men weren't one category either. One friend asked before helping with her bike; another assumed every repair was an audition for a masculinity contest. “I like the first nigga. The second can hold the flashlight if he learns to shut up.” She looked at Nia, then back. “And I don't want a woman to pick me because she thinks she's bought the reliable man package without a man in it.”

Nia put her glass down. “Good. I'm terrible at assembling packages. I like that you got excited explaining the brakes. You stopped checking whether everybody else was impressed.” Rae's face changed. Mine would have too. It was an intimate observation, and Nia offered it without making either of them a public symbol.

Shawna said she loved a man who sometimes confused being wanted with being required to run everything. I looked at her. “Baby.” “I'm speaking from the archive.” She squeezed my wrist. “Your tender parts aren't a leak in your authority, Aiden. Sometimes they're the only parts listening.”
I had a joke ready and let it go. That cost nothing and felt expensive.

Kit wanted to know what happened next. Not to the world; to our invitation, to the chairs, to the evening. Rae said she wanted the title left ridiculous if everyone remembered it wasn't a map of human beings. Kit could keep her entrance light. Rae could sit beside Nia. June could exist without becoming a footnote that repaired my race chart. The disagreement would not vanish because I found better paper.

I crossed out REPRESENTATIVE on the place cards. People could introduce themselves, and the caucuses could overlap. Kit kept her ribbon for the lamp. June kept the photograph. Dez kept the jacket, under protest. Rosa announced food, and nobody converted dinner into a reward for reaching ideological completion.
Shawna handed me the microphone at last. “One sentence.” I looked at the room. “The good crackers are over there.” Rae laughed first. Nigga, I had finally made an announcement I could substantiate.

ending.title: A Provisional Agenda and One Very Firm Dinner Reservation
paragraphs: We recovered the draft from the back of the welcome sign. The pen had emerged from a picture frame. Neither discovery reflected especially well on the host, but the papers were readable, the pen worked, and Kit had successfully negotiated her name being spelled correctly in the announcement. A summit needs achievable milestones.

Shawna and I came back from the corridor a few minutes later. I had given her actual attention, which improved her opinion of the evening and temporarily destroyed my ability to remember why I had purchased a smoke machine. Tank looked at my collar. “Negotiations going well?” “Private session.” “Nigga, your tie's private too. Put it back where it lives.”

Nia spread the draft on the now steady table. Rae had repaired the wobble with help from the hotel technician. Kit aimed the lamp. Nobody called the arrangement historic. It simply worked. June and Dez took opposite chairs, discovered that put them too far apart to discuss the photograph, and moved closer without asking which side they represented.

The draft was ridiculous in several places. I had proposed separate victory entrances for people who belonged to overlapping groups. Remy had a paragraph describing his fanfare as obligatory. He claimed he hadn't written obligatory, only essential. Velvet crossed out both and wrote PAID SHOW FIRST. Rosa added a clear meal time. Mercedes protected her soundcheck. Mika added an actual start time and took possession of the room controls.

Kit wanted her karaoke turn. Rae wanted snacks worth eating and a table nobody had to hold upright while signing. Nia wanted her legal contribution limited to the agreement for this evening, after which she would be free to enjoy it. I said everybody wanted something. Shawna touched my arm. “Yes, baby. That's why they came.” She wasn't delivering a lesson. She was asking me to stop sounding surprised.

June proposed putting the old Blue Comet claims on tomorrow's agenda. Dez objected that tomorrow had already been used as a settlement date since 1967. Nia suggested a separate little accounting session tonight. Both veterans accepted, provided it didn't interrupt the music. I sensed an opportunity to preside. Six people found useful reasons for me to remain standing away from the pen.

We agreed the order of the evening: games, food, financial terms, rooms, the stage, and a final agreement only when the words were actually ready. This was a provisional agenda. Nobody signed a grand coalition treaty. Remy played four seconds of his fanfare anyway. Velvet took his keyboard, played the final note properly, and handed it back with a kiss on his forehead.

Rae offered Nia a look at her bike before the next room. Nia said yes. I nearly volunteered a photographer. Shawna tightened her hand around mine until the thought passed safely through my body without becoming a purchase.

The hotel manager arrived carrying the financial statement. June leaned over to Dez. “Second war already got a casualty.” Dez looked at the total. “His deposit.” Nigga, the next campaign had begun before I'd finished enjoying the first truce.
